name: Cognitive Complexity Score
description: Estimates cognitive processing complexity using word frequency, sentence structure, and conceptual density measures.
mechanism:
This method detects AI-generated text by measuring cognitive processing complexity — how much mental effort a text demands from readers. AI text tends to maintain a narrow, comfortable complexity band, while human writing naturally varies between simple and complex passages:

1. **Lexical Complexity Layer**: The method measures word-level cognitive load using psycholinguistic norms: (a) word frequency — using the SUBTLEX-US database (Brysbaert & New, 2009), each word is assigned its Zipf frequency value (1–7 scale, where 7 = most frequent). Mean Zipf frequency for human text: 4.2–4.8; for AI text: 4.6–5.2 (AI prefers more common words). (b) Age of acquisition (AoA) — words learned later in life require more processing. Human text shows mean AoA of 6–9 years; AI text shows 5–7 years, using earlier-acquired vocabulary. (c) Orthographic neighborhood density — words with many similar-looking words are processed faster. AI text tends to use words with higher neighborhood density (N > 5), avoiding unusual word forms. The method computes a composite lexical complexity score: LC = w₁×(1/Zipf) + w₂×AoA + w₃×(1/N), where w₁, w₂, w₃ are empirically-derived weights.

2. **Syntactic Complexity Layer**: The method computes sentence-level processing difficulty: (a) dependency distance — the average linear distance between syntactically related words (measured in intervening words). Human text shows mean dependency distance of 3.5–5.0 words; AI text shows 2.5–3.5 words, producing shorter-distance, easier-to-process structures. (b) Yngve depth — the maximum left-branching depth at any point in a sentence, reflecting working memory load. Human text: mean Yngve depth 2.5–4.0; AI text: 1.8–2.8. (c) Integration cost — based on Gibson's (2000) Dependency Locality Theory, each new dependency incurs processing cost proportional to the distance to its head. Total integration cost per sentence is summed. (d) Surprise — the negative log probability of each word given preceding context (measured via GPT-2): mean surprisal for human text: 5–7 bits; AI text: 3–5 bits (more predictable because AI generates high-probability sequences).

3. **Conceptual Density Layer**: Beyond individual word and sentence difficulty, the method measures idea density: (a) propositional density — number of propositions (predicate-argument structures) per 100 words, computed from the dependency parse. Human text: 45–65 propositions per 100 words; AI text: 35–50 (AI text is often semantically diluted). (b) Referential density — number of unique referents introduced per 100 words. Human text: 8–15; AI text: 5–10 (AI repeats referents more). (c) Causal density — number of causal connections per 100 propositions. Human argumentative text: 15–25; AI text: 8–15 (AI text often lacks deeper causal reasoning, substituting correlation for causation). (d) New concept rate — rate at which genuinely new concepts (not previously mentioned in the discourse) are introduced. Human text shows declining new concept rate (fast introduction early, slower later); AI text shows flatter new concept introduction.

4. **Complexity Variation Pattern**: The key discriminative feature is not the overall complexity level but its variation across the text: (a) complexity time series — the method computes lexical, syntactic, and conceptual complexity per sentence, producing three time series. Human text shows high autocorrelation (smooth transitions between simple and complex passages, reflecting paragraph-level organization) and high overall variance (CV > 0.4). AI text shows low autocorrelation (complexity jumps randomly) and low variance (CV < 0.25 — staying in a narrow "comfort zone"). (b) Paragraph-level complexity arcs — human text often follows arc patterns within paragraphs (simple opening → complex middle → simple closing, or vice versa). The method detects these arcs using trend analysis. AI text shows flat or random complexity within paragraphs.
parameters:
Word frequency database: SUBTLEX-US (Zipf values)
Age of acquisition: Kuperman et al. 2012 norms
Mean Zipf human: 4.2–4.8
Mean Zipf AI: 4.6–5.2
Dependency distance human: 3.5–5.0
Dependency distance AI: 2.5–3.5
Proposition density human: 45–65 per 100 words
Surprisal human: 5–7 bits
Surprisal AI: 3–5 bits
Complexity CV human: > 0.4
Complexity CV AI: < 0.25
Minimum text length: 300 words
accuracy: 80–89% accuracy detecting AI-generated text via cognitive complexity analysis. Complexity variation pattern achieves AUC of 0.87. Surprisal analysis provides AUC of 0.85. Propositional density adds 2–4% improvement. Performance best for expository and argumentative text; effective across genres due to universal complexity variation patterns.
source: Gibson, E. (2000). The Dependency Locality Theory: A Distance-Based Theory of Linguistic Complexity. In Image, Language, Brain (MIT Press).
useCase: Detecting AI-generated text through unnatural complexity uniformity. Assessing readability and cognitive load for educational content. Evaluating writing sophistication in academic integrity checking. Analyzing text difficulty calibration for audience-appropriate communication.
strengths:
• Multi-level analysis captures complexity at lexical, syntactic, and conceptual layers
• Complexity variation is a powerful meta-feature independent of absolute complexity
• Psycholinguistic norms are well-validated through decades of research
• Surprisal-based measures directly relate to language model behavior
• Works across genres due to universal human writing variability patterns
limitations:
• Psycholinguistic norms are primarily available for English
• Text genre strongly influences expected complexity levels
• Very short texts may not show sufficient complexity variation
• Deliberately simplified text (easy readers) may mimic AI patterns
• Edited and polished human text may show reduced complexity variation
